titleZh: 农业技术采用与实施：从“提供”到“落地”的差距
summaryZh: 本文由Vision Technology Management CEO Dave Swain撰写，指出农业技术产品和服务虽不断增多，但“提供”不等于“销售”和“执行”。通过对比两家零售点的案例，揭示销售团队主动推广与被动等待的显著差异。文章提出技术采用率低的四个原因，并给出实施计划中应包含的四个关键要素，特别强调佣金结构对技术销售激励的缺失。最后呼吁企业制定贯穿购买前、中、后的完整计划，将技术真正转化为业务价值。
featuredReason: 本文直击农业技术落地难的核心痛点，提供了可操作的实施框架和激励方案建议，对智慧畜牧企业推动技术商业化具有重要借鉴意义。
contentFull:
By Dave SwainCEO | Vision Technology Management 

 

 Share

 

 

 

 

 

 Increases in the offering of technology products and services continues to be encouraging, especially now, when a slowing economy makes better decision-making more critical than ever.

 But offering a service is not the same as selling it or executing on it.

 I worked with two retail locations from the same company, similar geography, similar demographics, similar product line-ups. One location had roughly 5,000 acres enrolled in its precision program. The other location had nearly 20,000 (this was mid-to-late 1990s).

 When I learned about the significant difference between the locations, I started asking questions. I found that the location with 5,000 acres was offering the services and had the attitude that if the growers want it, they will ask for it. The location that had almost 20,000 acres in its program had salespeople actively out in the field, selling growers on the value of the program, walking them through the agronomics, and helping them execute on the plans they’d developed together.

 Offering a program is very different than selling and executing on a program.

 So, why aren’t we doing more than just offering? Is it a lack of trust in the product or service that we don’t want to take the risk on something that’s unproven? Is it that the product or service was bought by someone in the organization, handed down to the sales team, and now sits on a list of things they’re supposed to sell but don’t really believe in? Or is it another over-promised solution that’s left people skeptical or even cynical?

 Whatever the reason, the result is the same: The technology sits on the shelf while the investment goes unrealized.

 Part of the problem — and I’ve written about this before — is that the right questions aren’t being asked before the purchase is made, and there’s rarely a structured implementation plan afterward.

 Here are four things that should be a part of an implementation plan.

 Is everyone on board? Teams need to believe in what they are selling, and that trust and confidence needs to be built before the launch, not after. One person in this process can make all the difference. Good or bad.

 What will be the new processes to implement the new product or service? What changes in the day-to-day workflow?

 How does it integrate with the current offerings? If the new offering duplicates or conflicts with the current business, confusion follows.

 What is the commission structure for the new offerings?

 That last point, I believe, is one of the biggest sticking points for technology adoption and implementation. Commission structures haven’t changed too much over the years. Commissions are still significantly based on the core products of the business, whether that is crop inputs or equipment.

 Don’t misunderstand me. The core products and services are what pay the bills. But I continue to hear companies tout that they are “technology companies” but don’t incentivize their sales teams to sell the technology. So, it just becomes an offering or just included with the rest of the program … and the value isn’t truly realized.

 New offerings are great for the business. They keep the company relevant to its customers and engaged in the industry. But, as I mentioned earlier, the economy is a little slow right now and return on investment is vital to any business.

 Offering something new just doesn’t cut it anymore. You need a plan before you make the purchase, during the purchase, and after the purchase to make the technology a viable, saleable product or service.

 Reminds me of the old saying that became cliché but I’m going to use it anyway. “Plan your work. Work your plan. If you fail to plan, you plan to fail.”

 The technology is there. The need is there. What’s missing, too often, is the plan to turn an offering into a business.

 Editor’s Note: This article was originally published on CropLife.com, a sister brand of the Global Ag Tech Initiative.

translationZh:
技术产品和服务的供应持续增长，这令人鼓舞，尤其是在当前经济放缓、更好的决策比以往任何时候都更为关键的时刻。

但提供服务与销售服务或执行服务是两回事。

我曾与同一家公司的两个零售点合作，它们地理位置相似、人口结构相似、产品线相似。一个点在其精准项目中登记了大约5000英亩土地。另一个点则接近20000英亩（这是1990年代中后期的情况）。

当我了解到两个点之间的显著差异后，我开始提出问题。我发现，拥有5000英亩的那个点只是在提供服务，并且持有一种态度：如果种植者想要，他们会主动来问。而拥有近20000英亩的那个点，销售人员积极深入田间，向种植者推销该项目的价值，带他们了解农艺细节，并帮助他们执行共同制定的计划。

提供项目与销售并执行项目是完全不同的。

那么，为什么我们不仅仅停留在“提供”层面呢？是因为对产品或服务缺乏信任，不想冒险尝试未经证实的东西吗？是因为产品或服务由组织中的某个人购买，然后交给销售团队，现在只是列在他们应该销售但内心并不真正相信的清单上？还是因为又一个过度承诺的解决方案让人们持怀疑甚至愤世嫉俗的态度？

无论原因是什么，结果都一样：技术被束之高阁，投资无法实现。

问题的一部分——我之前也写过——在于购买前没有提出正确的问题，购买后也几乎没有结构化的实施计划。

以下是实施计划中应包含的四项内容。

**是否所有人都认同？** 团队需要相信他们所销售的东西，这种信任和信心需要在发布前建立，而不是发布后。在这个过程中，一个人就能带来天壤之别。好或坏。

**实施新产品或服务的新流程是什么？** 日常工作流程中会发生哪些变化？

**它如何与现有产品集成？** 如果新产品与现有业务重复或冲突，就会带来混乱。

**新产品的佣金结构是什么？**

最后一点，我认为是技术采用和实施的最大障碍之一。佣金结构多年来变化不大。佣金仍然主要基于企业的核心产品，无论是农资还是设备。

不要误解我的意思。核心产品和服务是支付账单的关键。但我不断听到企业宣称自己是“科技公司”，却不激励销售团队销售技术。因此，技术仅仅成为一种“提供”或包含在其余项目中……其价值并未真正实现。

新产品对企业来说很好。它们让公司与客户保持相关性，并参与行业。但正如我之前提到的，当前经济有些缓慢，投资回报对任何企业都至关重要。

仅仅提供新产品已经不够了。你需要一个计划，在购买前、购买中和购买后都制定计划，才能使技术成为一种可行的、可销售的产品或服务。

这让我想起一句老话，虽然已经老套，但我还是要用：“计划你的工作，执行你的计划。如果你不计划，你就在计划失败。”

技术就在那里。需求就在那里。但往往缺失的是将“提供”转化为业务的计划。

Technology investments deliver value only when retailers have a clear plan to sell, implement, and support them.
